sections.h2: Where do I record a deed in Venango County, PA?
sections.html:
Deeds are recorded at the Venango County Register and Recorder office in the county courthouse at 1168 Liberty Street, Franklin, PA 16323. Mail goes to P.O. Box 831 in Franklin. The office is open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., except legal holidays.

The same elected office also serves as Register of Wills and Clerk of Orphans' Court, so probate filings, marriage licenses and real estate recordings all run through one courthouse counter. A seller dealing with an inherited house will often visit for both reasons.

sections.h2: Can Venango County deeds be recorded electronically?
sections.html:
Yes. The county says electronic filing of real estate documents is handled by CSC eRecording Solutions, reachable at 866-652-0111. Title companies and attorneys commonly use e-recording because it skips the courthouse trip and the mail time, and it fits well when buyer and seller sign in different places.

The Register and Recorder's page does not print the recording fees in the text of the page. It tells filers to contact the office for fees or a fee schedule, and the county also posts a Recorder of Deeds fee schedule dated November 2025 in its document library. Call the office for the exact total on your deed before you send payment.

sections.h2: How is realty transfer tax handled in a Venango County sale?
sections.html:
The recorder collects it with the deed. Pennsylvania's state rate is 1 percent of the value, and the Department of Revenue says the grantor and grantee are jointly and severally liable. Local governments may add their own tax and divide it between school districts and municipalities.

  • Certain family transfers, transfers to government and nonprofit bodies, and property passed by will or intestacy are exempt.
  • Fifteen percent of state collections go to the Keystone Recreation, Park and Conservation Fund, and the rest goes to the General Fund.
  • The sales contract sets who pays in practice, so read that clause before you sign.

Venango County has two cities, Franklin and Oil City, plus boroughs and townships, and the local share depends on where the parcel sits. Ask the recorder which municipality and school district your parcel falls in before you work out your net proceeds.

sections.h2: Where did Venango County get its oil history?
sections.html:
Venango County was created in 1800 and organized in 1805, and its name comes from a Native American word for otter. The county is tied to the start of the oil industry. On August 28, 1859, George Bissell and Edwin L. Drake used the first successful drilling rig near Titusville, and the well sat less than a mile inside the Venango County line. Oil boom towns followed, among them Franklin, Oil City and the now vanished Pithole City.

The industry also shaped the land. French Creek, which runs 117 miles, joins the Allegheny River near Franklin, and Riverfront Park in Franklin sits at that meeting point. A seller with an older house in the two cities should expect a buyer's inspector to look hard at the foundation, wiring and plumbing.

sections.h2: What do Venango County housing numbers look like?
sections.html:
Venango County has been losing residents for decades. Its population peaked at 65,328 in 1950 and stood at 50,454 in 2020. The Census Bureau estimates 49,346 as of July 1, 2025, down 2.2% from the 2020 base. By 2018 estimates, Oil City (9,897), Cranberry Township (6,789), Franklin (6,231) and Sugar Creek borough (5,008) were the largest places.

sections.h2: How do I look up real estate tax rates in Venango County?
sections.html:
The county publishes a Real Estate Tax Millages page with a PDF for every year from 2005 through 2026. Check the latest sheet for your municipality and school district, since the millage that applies to a house depends on where it sits. Ask the county's Tax Assessment Office, also in the courthouse complex, about the assessed value behind that bill.

A buyer will ask for this information, and it helps to have the last tax bill in hand when you talk to a title company. If you want to sell without fixing the house first, a direct cash purchase as is can work in this county, where repair costs on an older home can exceed what the market will return.

faqs.q: What are the Venango County Recorder of Deeds office hours?
faqs.a: The office is open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., except legal holidays. It is in the courthouse at 1168 Liberty Street in Franklin.

faqs.q: Can I e-record a deed in Venango County?
faqs.a: Yes. The county names CSC eRecording Solutions as the processor of electronic real estate filings, at 866-652-0111. Your title company or attorney can usually set this up.

faqs.q: Where can I find the Venango County recording fees?
faqs.a: The county posts a Recorder of Deeds fee schedule from November 2025 in its document library, and the Register and Recorder's page tells you to contact the office for fees. Call before you send a check.

faqs.q: Who handles probate for a Venango County house?
faqs.a: The Register of Wills handles probate and collects inheritance tax for the Commonwealth. In Venango County that office is combined with the Recorder and the Clerk of Orphans' Court.

faqs.q: How much is realty transfer tax in Venango County?
faqs.a: The state charges 1 percent of the value. Local shares are added by the municipality and school district, so ask the recorder for the combined rate that applies to your parcel.
